Keywords: Somewhere, Chelsea, And

outputs.L1:
Somewhere in Chelsea, early summer evening—
Walking through the twilight toward the docks,
I thought I glimpsed Robinson ahead of me.
From an uncurtained second-story window,
A radio was playing *There's a Small Hotel*;
A kite twisted above darkened rooftops
And slow, drifting birds.

We were alone there, he and I,
The sole inhabitants of that empty street.
Beneath a sign for Natural Bloom Cigars,
While traffic lights clicked softly through the dusk
From red to green, he paused
Before a window where a plaster Venus,
Modeling a surgical truss,
Gazed out at the eastbound traffic.

(Yet Robinson, I knew, was out of town—
He summers at a place in Maine,
Sometimes Fire Island, sometimes the Cape;
He leaves in June and doesn't return till after Labor Day.)

Still, I nearly called out, "Robinson!"
But there was no chance. Just as I passed,
Turning my head to catch his face,
His own head turned with mine
And fixed me with dilated, terrible eyes
That froze the blood in my veins.
His voice reached me like an echo out of darkness:

"I thought I saw the whirlpool opening.
I kicked all night against a bolted door.
You must have followed me from Astor Place.
An empty sheet of paper drifts down at the end.
And then a day as vast as yesterday, doubled,
Unrolled its horror across my face
Until it blotted out—"
outputs.L2:
In a corner of Chelsea, as early summer settled in, I made my way through fading light toward the waterfront, and thought I glimpsed Robinson walking just ahead of me. From a window left bare on the second floor, a radio drifted the tune of *There's a Small Hotel*; overhead, a kite spun and turned above darkened roofs while birds floated lazily by.

The two of us seemed to have that deserted street entirely to ourselves. Beneath a sign advertising Natural Bloom Cigars, as the traffic signals shifted quietly from red to green in the dimming light, he paused before a storefront window. Inside, a plaster statue of Venus, fitted with a truss, stared blankly out at cars heading east.

Yet I knew this couldn't be Robinson—he was supposed to be away, spending his summers in Maine, or perhaps Fire Island, or the Cape, always gone from June until after Labor Day. Still, I nearly shouted his name aloud.

But there was no opportunity. Just as I drew even with him and turned to catch a glimpse of his face, he turned his own head at the same moment, and his eyes—wide, dilated, filled with something like dread—locked onto mine and froze me where I stood. When he spoke, his words reached me as though bouncing back from some hollow distance:

"I believed I was watching a whirlpool begin to swirl. All night long I struggled against a door that wouldn't give. You must have trailed me all the way from Astor Place. In the end, an empty sheet of paper drifts downward. Then a day, doubled in size like the one before, spread its terror across my face until it swallowed—"
outputs.L3:
It was one of those Chelsea evenings when the light seems reluctant to leave, clinging to the tops of the plane trees and the old brick facades near the river, as though dusk itself were stalling for time. I had walked down toward the docks without any particular purpose, the kind of aimless walking that empties the mind rather than fills it, and it was there, on a narrow street I couldn't have named, that I saw him.

He was perhaps thirty yards ahead, standing half in shadow beneath a doorway, and everything about his posture—the slight forward lean, the way he held his hands loosely at his sides—belonged unmistakably to Robinson. The street around us seemed to conspire in strangeness: somewhere a radio played through an open window, the melody thin and warped by distance, arriving in fragments that didn't quite cohere into a song. Above the rooftops a child's kite drifted untethered, no child in sight to claim it, tugged by currents I couldn't feel at street level. Further along, a traffic light cycled through its colours for a street empty of cars, red to amber to green, patient and absurd, as if performing for no one. The whole scene had the quality of a dream remembered slightly wrong—familiar shapes rearranged into something faintly wrong.

And yet I knew, with the flat certainty one reserves for facts rather than impressions, that this could not be Robinson. He had told me himself, weeks before, that he was leaving London for the summer, retreating to some coastal town whose name I'd already forgotten, escaping the city's heat and its obligations. He was not here. He could not be here. The logic of it was simple and complete, and I repeated it to myself even as my feet slowed, even as my eyes refused to look away from the figure in the doorway.

Despite this certainty—perhaps because of it, some perverse need to test the impossible—I felt his name rise in my throat, half-formed, almost spoken. I did not call out. But something in my hesitation must have carried anyway, some disturbance in the stillness, because the figure turned.

What I saw in that turning I have found difficult to describe since, and harder still to forget. It was not simply that the face resembled Robinson's, though it did, uncannily so. It was the eyes—wide, fixed, holding an expression that belonged to no ordinary recognition or greeting. There was something pleading in them, and something else beneath the pleading that I can only call terror, or perhaps the aftermath of terror, the look of a man who has seen something and not yet finished seeing it. The shock of that gaze went through me like cold water; I felt my own breath catch, my legs suddenly uncertain beneath me.

Then he spoke, though "spoke" seems too orderly a word for what emerged—a voice broken into pieces, catching on itself, the words arriving out of sequence as though assembled by someone relearning language.

"The water," he said, "it doesn't stop—it keeps coming up the stairs, up through the floor, and the rooms keep changing, they keep becoming other rooms—" He stopped, started again. "I saw my own hands and they weren't—they were someone else's hands, moving without me, and the light kept—the light kept folding in on itself like paper, like it was trying to become dark and couldn't finish—"

He pressed his palms against his temples as though to hold something in, or keep something out. "Don't let them turn the lights green," he said, quite suddenly, his eyes flicking toward the traffic signal at the end of the street. "Not yet. Not until I've finished counting."

I stood frozen, unable to answer him, unable even to fully believe I was hearing him, while the radio music drifted on unbothered, and the kite continued its slow, purposeless circling above us, and the light—inevitably, indifferently—turned green.
outputs.L4:
# On the Poem's Spectral Encounter in Chelsea

The poem opens in that liminal hour when day surrenders to night, when Chelsea's streets grow uncertain in their outlines and the city itself seems to hold its breath. The narrator moves through this half-light like a man walking through his own memory, and it is in this uncertain atmosphere that he catches sight of a figure who seems, unmistakably, to be Robinson—Robinson who has been absent, who exists now only as rumor and recollection among those who once knew him. The recognition arrives not as certainty but as a kind of vertigo: is this truly the man, returned from wherever he has gone, or is he merely a projection summoned by the narrator's own loneliness and longing?

The poem refuses to answer this question cleanly, and this refusal is precisely its genius. Chelsea's brownstones lean in with a watchful, almost sentient quality; lamplight pools on wet pavement in a way that suggests illumination without clarity; shadows stretch and multiply until the narrator can no longer trust the evidence of his own eyes. Every physical detail of the urban landscape becomes suspect, complicit in an atmosphere where the boundary between what is witnessed and what is merely imagined grows perilously thin. The reader, like the narrator, is left suspended between competing realities—did this encounter happen, or has grief and isolation conjured a hallucination wearing a familiar face?

This uncertainty builds toward the poem's true center of gravity: the moment of confrontation with the double itself. Here the poem abandons ambiguity for something far more visceral and disturbing. The figure who may or may not be Robinson does not offer calm reassurance or simple explanation. Instead, he delivers a confession marked by raw terror—a voice that seems to echo and fracture even as it speaks, as though the speaker cannot fully inhabit his own words. This is not a man calmly explaining his absence; this is a consciousness caught in the act of dissolving, describing its own psychic disintegration in real time. The horror lies not in supernatural trappings but in the utterly human dread of watching identity itself come apart at the seams—the self splitting, doubling, losing its coherent center.

What might have remained a minor anecdote of mistaken identity in a poorer poem becomes, through this uncanny doubling, something far more profound: a meditation on the fragility of selfhood itself. The narrator's encounter with "Robinson" forces confrontation with unsettling questions the poem never resolves. Is the double a genuine manifestation of Robinson's fractured psyche, externalized and given voice? Is he instead a mirror held up to the narrator's own suppressed fears about identity, memory, and the possibility of one's own dissolution? Or is the entire episode simply evidence of the narrator's unreliable perception, a symptom of his own encroaching paranoia?

The poem's lasting power derives precisely from this irresolution. By refusing to stabilize into either straightforward realism or clear allegory, it captures something essential about modern urban existence—the way anonymity and isolation can erode the boundaries of selfhood, the way a chance encounter in half-light can crack open existential terrors we spend most of our waking lives suppressing. The confession that closes the poem, terrified and echoing, lingers precisely because it could belong to anyone: Robinson, the narrator, or the reader themselves, caught for a moment in Chelsea's twilight, uncertain whether the face they glimpse in a stranger is recognition or reflection, memory or hallucination, another man's ruin or a premonition of their own.
outputs.L5:
# Somewhere in Chelsea

Somewhere between the cobblestone streets and the quiet hum of King's Road, Chelsea holds onto its character like an old photograph—slightly faded, but unmistakably itself. This London neighborhood has always existed at an intersection: of old money and new art, of tradition and rebellion, of quiet residential calm and bursts of cultural energy.

Walk along the Thames here, and you'll find yourself somewhere that feels both timeless and alive. The Chelsea Physic Garden, tucked away since 1673, offers a green sanctuary where medicinal plants have grown for centuries. Not far away, the Saatchi Gallery pulses with contemporary art, proving that Chelsea has never been content to simply preserve its past—it insists on adding to it.

And that's perhaps what defines this place best: the "and." Chelsea is elegant townhouses and punk rock history, where the Sex Pistols once roamed the same streets now lined with boutique shops. It's Sunday afternoon tea and Saturday night gallery openings. It's the football club that bears its name, uniting thousands in blue and white, and the quiet residential squares where little seems to have changed in a hundred years.

Somewhere in the details—a well-worn doorstep, a flower box overflowing with blooms, the particular slant of afternoon light on the river—Chelsea reveals itself not as one thing, but as many things existing simultaneously. It is history and modernity, wealth and artistry, permanence and change, all coexisting in a few square miles that continue to captivate anyone who takes the time to wander through.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal urban poem in the style of Weldon Kees' "Robinson" poems, featuring a mysterious doppelganger encountered on a city street at dusk.
counterfactuals.output:
**Harmon at Dusk**

The lights come on in the windows above the appliance store,
and Harmon, buttoning his coat against no particular cold,
sees himself crossing at the light three blocks ahead—
same hat, same walk, the same left hand
patting the same pocket for a light.

He does not call out. The city does not encourage this.
Somewhere a bus exhales and pulls away
carrying the ordinary evening off toward the river,
and the man ahead turns the corner
into a street that Harmon's memory does not keep.

*He has my overcoat,* Harmon thinks, *the gray one
with the button gone, replaced with black.
He has my slight limp, favoring the right,
souvenir of a war I may have invented.*
The neon of a bar sign write and rewrites itself: OPEN, OPEN.

Later, in the vestibule of his apartment building,
he finds a single glove, not his, though it fits.
The mailbox key turns twice before it turns at all.
Upstairs, the radiator speaks in its old tongue,
and someone, one floor up, is walking in his socks
the exact number of steps from window to door
that Harmon walks, some nights, when he can't sleep.

In the bathroom mirror, shaving, he pauses—
the face gives nothing back but the usual late report:
tired eyes, a small cut healing near the throat,
the particular slackness of a man
who has misplaced something and stopped looking for it.

Outside, the streetlamps gather their small congregations of moths.
Harmon turns off the bathroom light.
In the dark of the hallway a shape is standing
that does not announce itself as anyone's,
and the coat it wears is torn in the same place his is torn,
and neither of them speaks,
and neither of them is surprised.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a noir-tinged free verse poem set in 1950s Manhattan where the speaker glimpses a man named Robinson who then turns and speaks in unsettling, fragmented lines.
counterfactuals.output:
**Robinson, Later**

Rain comes down Lexington like a verdict,
and I see him under the Longines clock,
collar up, the color of wet ash—
Robinson, or the idea of Robinson,
standing where the El used to scream past
before they tore the iron out
and called it progress.

He's counting something on his fingers.
Not money. Never money.

The automat glows behind him, all that chrome
and small locked windows full of pie,
and I think: a man could disappear
into a city like a nickel into a slot,
and nobody would call it a crime.

I know him from the papers, maybe.
Or the bar on Forty-Ninth
where the mirror doubles everyone
and nobody minds.

He turns.

*"You again,"* he says, though we've never met—
*"or someone wearing you. It happens.
The suits get tailored. The names
get passed around like matchbooks."*

Smoke from a cigarette that isn't lit.

*"I had a wife. I think.
There was a window, and a bridge, and after that
just the sound a name makes
when you stop answering to it."*

The rain keeps its own counsel.
Somewhere a radio is selling toothpaste
to an empty room.

*"You're looking for the man,"* he says,
*"but the man was never the point.
Ask the coat. Ask the hat.
Ask the shape the streetlight makes
where a man should be standing."*

He steps back into the neon
the way a fact steps back into rumor,
and the automat door swings shut
on its small bright cells of pie,

and I'm alone with the wet iron ghosts
of a train that isn't there,
counting the blocks to nowhere
on fingers that aren't mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that blends John Ashbery's dreamlike imagery with a narrative about mistaking a stranger for an old acquaintance near the docks at twilight.
counterfactuals.output:
**Harbor Mistaken**

The light was doing that thing again, unbuttoning itself
along the pier's wet spine, and I thought: there—
isn't that Marcus, come back from whatever country
keeps the people we've lost track of, the way
a coat keeps the shape of shoulders after the body's gone.

He was standing near the bollards, or something
was standing there, wearing his posture like a rumor.
The gulls had opinions about this. The water
kept revising its face. I called out a name
that may have belonged to someone else entirely,
some other twilight, some other pier
where the same brand of loneliness was being sold
at a discount, on account of the season closing.

He turned. Of course he turned—everyone turns,
eventually, toward the sound of their almost-name,
even strangers, especially strangers, who carry
in their turning all the people they are not.
It wasn't him. It was someone wearing the evening
the way Marcus used to wear his doubt, loosely,
like a jacket he'd stolen from a taller man.

We stood there, the stranger and I, two accidents
of resemblance, while behind us the boats
knocked against each other like unfinished sentences.
He asked if I was lost. I said I was only
early for a meeting that had already happened,
years ago, with someone who no longer answers
to the weather I keep mistaking for his name.

The dock lights flickered on, one by one,
practicing their small, deliberate miracles.
Somewhere a horn sounded the shape of departure.
I apologized for the confusion of my life,
for expecting the past to wear a familiar coat
and stroll toward me out of the failing light—

as if memory were a kind of navigation,
as if the tide, in its patient revisions,
might return what it borrowed, unbruised,
still answering to the old, mistaken name.

We shook hands. His was warmer than I expected,
the warmth of someone who has never
been anyone else, who has always been
exactly this stranger, this gift
of not being who I needed him to be.

I walked back through the evening's rough draft,
past the boats still arguing among themselves,
past the gulls revising their complaints,
carrying the shape of my mistake like a lantern—
useless in daylight, but here, now,
lighting the exact, particular dark
where all the people I have lost
continue, faithfully, to almost arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem featuring recurring character "Robinson," incorporating specific sensory details like a radio playing a jazz standard, a cigar shop sign, and a mannequin in a shop window, ending on an ominous, unfinished line.
counterfactuals.output:
**Robinson at Dusk**

Robinson walks the avenue where the cigar shop's
wooden sign, its painted Indian chief, has faded
to the color of an old bruise, and the radio
in the window plays "Body and Soul" for no one,
the saxophone bending like a question
nobody in this city wants answered.

Robinson does not look at the mannequin
in Feldman's window—the one in the green dress,
her painted eyes fixed on some middle distance,
her wrist cocked at an angle no living wrist
would hold for thirty years of afternoons—
but he feels her watching anyway,
the way you feel a name you've almost forgotten
scratching at the door behind your teeth.

The trumpet on the radio goes quiet.
A man's voice reads the evening scores.
Robinson checks his watch. Robinson checks
the street behind him, empty as a drawer.
Robinson touches his coat pocket, where the letter
sits unopened, warm as something living,
and thinks of how the chief above the cigar shop
has been pointing west since 1949,
one arm raised, its finger snapped clean off,
gesturing at nothing, at the same
dead patch of sky, at whatever
comes for a man who stops

to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an eerie, atmospheric poem about identity and doubling, where the narrator encounters someone who should be out of town, and the encounter ends with a chilling, cryptic monologue.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Guest

I saw you at the corner store on Elm,
buying milk you don't drink,
though you told me Tuesday
you'd be in the mountains until Friday,
your phone dark by choice,
your absence a gift you were giving yourself.

But there you were—
same crooked part in your hair,
same way of holding the door
a half-second too long,
as if unsure the world would let you through.

I called your name.
You turned like water turns,
all surface, no depth to catch the light,
and smiled with a mouth
that remembered how,
but had forgotten why.

"You're supposed to be gone," I said.

"I am gone," you answered,
and the bell above the door
rang once, though no one moved.

We stood there in the cereal aisle
while the fluorescent lights
hummed a note too low for comfort,
and you leaned in close enough
that I could smell nothing at all—
not soap, not skin, not time.

"Let me tell you," you whispered,
"about the ones who leave.
We don't go anywhere.
We fold ourselves into the spaces
you stopped looking at—
the back of the closet,
the space between your ribs,
the pause before you answer the phone.

You think a person is a place
you can point to on a map.
But we are weather.
We are the version of you
that stayed home
when you went out,
that answered when you didn't call,
that is, right now,
wearing your face
somewhere you have never been.

Go home.
Check the mirror.
Tell me which one of us
forgot to come back."

Then the milk was on the shelf,
the door unmoving,
and I was alone
with my hand still raised
in a wave
that no one was left to answer.

I did not check the mirror.

Some nights, I still don't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
